section_intro: A shawl began the inquiry. These twelve readings follow it into the lives around Niyamgiri: households and fields, makers and markets, classrooms and songs. Read them in sequence, or begin with a person or question that draws you in.

opening.title: A shawl, and the questions it opened
opening.summary: At a dinner at Sabyasachi Supper Club, Ahimanikya Satapathy noticed the cloth and bought a shawl. The encounter led to weeks of reading about its makers and their lives, with a visit to Niyamgiri still ahead.

closing.title: Looking again
closing.summary: The shawl remains a source of delight, but the reading has brought names, work and time into view. Ahimanikya returns to the questions it opened, inviting readers to remember a person and look again at a familiar object.

parts.title: Place and people
parts.intro: Begin with the decisions that shape a household: what to plant, how to speak for land and what makes a home dependable.

chapters.summary: Singari Jakesika’s account begins with a change in what her family grew and ate. Her experience opens a wider story of household choices, shared work and learning in Niyamgiri.

Suresh Wadaka explains cultivated slopes through the roots of their crops. Accounts of the 2013 village assemblies then follow people insisting that their claims to the landscape be heard and accurately recorded.
Mana Manjhi wanted a roof that would shelter her and her grandson through storms. Her relief opens questions about building, repairs and the choices residents make about services and their homes.

parts.title: Growing and sharing
parts.intro: Follow the work that keeps food moving between fields, forests, households and markets, and the people who decide what to keep, share or sell.

chapters.summary: Dasara Kadraka worried about millet varieties disappearing from local fields. Accounts of priestesses, growers and messengers follow the conversations, journeys and planting that keep seeds in circulation between households.

Padmavati Paleka’s seasonal foods and Madhabi Jani’s learning trips bring gathering and household meals into view. These Rayagada accounts span several communities, connecting forest foods, home gardens and purchases without treating them as exclusively Dongria experiences.
Telo Wadaka’s journey to market connects growing produce with finding a buyer. Other growers describe long selling days, unsold harvests and the storage and processing they wanted closer to home.

parts.title: Cloth and its makers
parts.intro: Move from the finished wrap to the people who teach embroidery, weave its ground, make ornaments and explain what their work means.

chapters.summary: Kumri Sikoka learned embroidery from her father’s sister, while Site Jakesika valued the independence selling her work could bring. Their accounts lead through cloth, stitches, attributed meanings and questions about what reaches the maker.

An embroiderer’s katri can trim thread as well as adorn her hair. Accounts of Ghasi metalworking households and museum objects follow the relationships between making, selling and wearing, while leaving room for a wearer’s explanation.

Ram Hial’s weaving in Jhigidi and Kapilo Mahanta’s Kotpad profile introduce distinct textile traditions. Following base cloth, embroidery and dyed yarn shows why shared colours or a promotional platform do not make their production histories interchangeable.

parts.title: Learning, language and song
parts.intro: End with people helping others understand a lesson, work with familiar words and remember a singer’s voice.

chapters.summary: Mukteswar Wadaka brought free tuition to children in his village during lockdown. Students, teachers and women returning to study describe encouragement and familiar words alongside ambitions, family ties and concerns about learning away from home.

Phulamani Jani’s regional teaching account begins with children responding to Kuvi. Primers, language contributors and Prasanna Sree’s devised Jatapu script introduce different ways of working with words, without establishing which resources a Dongria classroom uses.

Singers helped Priyadarshini Mishra record, translate and explain songs and stories. Dambu Praska’s remembered voice, students’ accounts and film credits follow how songs travel while keeping attention on the people who sing and those who listen.
